walkthroughs.body_html:
Unit AS 2: Composing — a core area of A-Level Music.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Unit AS 2: Composing brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Unit AS 2: Composing.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Several notes sung to a single syllable of text is called what?
options: Syllabic setting
Melismatic setting
Recitative
Sprechstimme

mcqs.q: An ostinato is best described as what?
options: A persistently repeated pattern
A sudden key change
A slow introduction
An improvised cadenza

mcqs.q: Which chords are the primary triads in a major key?
options: I, IV and V
II, III and VI
I, III and VII
IV, VI and VII

mcqs.q: A balanced classical-style melody often pairs an antecedent phrase with what?
options: A consequent phrase of matching length
A drum fill
A second time signature
An unrelated new theme

mcqs.q: What is melisma in word setting?
options: Cadences appear only in vocal music.
Melisma means many syllables sung quickly on a single repeated note.
Melisma is the gap left between two verses of a song.
Several notes sung to one syllable of text, often used to highlight an expressive word.

mcqs.q: Should a composition include as many different ideas as possible?
options: Melisma is the gap left between two verses of a song.
A composition may legally contain only one idea.
No - strong pieces develop a small number of ideas thoroughly, creating unity as well as contrast.
More new ideas always make a composition more interesting.

mcqs.q: Do cadences only occur at the very end of a piece?
options: Cadences appear only in vocal music.
A cadence is only the final two chords of the whole composition.
A composition may legally contain only one idea.
No - cadences punctuate the ends of phrases throughout, like commas and full stops in prose.
